name: Main idea
sub: What the whole thing is about
rule: The main idea is the one point every sentence helps make. Details are the examples and facts that back it up.
trick: Finish this sentence after reading: "The author mostly wants me to know that ___." If your answer only fits one sentence, it's a detail, not the main idea.
passage: Octopuses are escape artists. They can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak, which is the only hard part of their body. Aquarium keepers have found them in neighboring tanks, in drainpipes, and once on the floor of a lab, heading for the door.

examples.text: Octopuses are very good at escaping.
examples.note: Every sentence supports this.

examples.text: An octopus was found on a lab floor.
examples.note: True, but it's one example, not the point.

another.text: Imagine texting a friend what the paragraph said, in one message. You'd skip the drainpipes and the lab floor and just say "octopuses escape from everything." That one message is the main idea.
another.example:
Details: beak, tanks, drainpipes, lab floor
Main idea: they escape from everything

questions.passage: Honeybees communicate with a dance. A bee that finds flowers returns to the hive and waggles in a figure eight. The angle of the dance tells the others which direction to fly, and the length of the waggle tells them how far.
questions.stem: What is the main idea?
options: Bees fly in a figure eight to find flowers.
Bees use a dance to tell each other where flowers are.
The length of a waggle shows distance.
questions.why: Every sentence is about the dance as a message. The angle and the length are details that back it up.

questions.passage: The town library did not close during the storm. Volunteers kept the generator running, handed out blankets, and let families charge their phones. By morning, forty people had slept in the reading room.
questions.stem: What is the main idea?
options: The library became a shelter during the storm.
Forty people slept in the reading room.
Volunteers know how to run a generator.
questions.why: Blankets, phones and forty sleepers all show the same thing: the library turned into a shelter.

questions.passage: Cast iron pans last for generations, but they ask for care. They must be dried right away so they do not rust, and they should be wiped with a thin coat of oil after each use. Soap, once forbidden, is fine in small amounts.
questions.stem: What is the main idea?
options: Soap is fine on cast iron.
Cast iron lasts a long time if you take care of it.
questions.why: The first sentence states it, and the rest explain what that care looks like.

questions.passage: Many people think camels store water in their humps. The humps are actually fat. A camel survives long trips because its body loses water slowly and its blood cells can swell without bursting when it finally drinks.
questions.stem: What is the main idea?
options: Camels survive without water because of how their bodies work, not their humps.
Camel humps are made of fat.
Camels drink a lot of water at once.
questions.why: The passage corrects a myth and gives the real reason. The fat and the blood cells are the details.

questions.passage: A good password is long before it is clever. Four random words beat one word with a number swapped in, because length is what makes guessing slow. "purple-tractor-moon-sandwich" would take a computer centuries; "P@ssw0rd" takes seconds.
questions.stem: What is the main idea?
options: Longer passwords are stronger than clever ones.
questions.why: The two example passwords exist to prove the point about length.

name: Finding the detail
sub: The answer is in the text, word for word
rule: A detail question asks what the text actually says. The answer is in there; your job is to find it and match it, not to remember or guess.
trick: Put your finger on the exact words in the passage that prove your answer. If you can't, you're guessing.
passage: The first bicycles had no pedals. Riders sat on a wooden frame and pushed along the ground with their feet, like a scooter you sit on. Pedals were added about forty years later, in the 1860s.

examples.text: How did early riders move? They pushed with their feet.
examples.note: Finger lands on "pushed along the ground with their feet."

examples.text: How did early riders move? They pedaled slowly.
examples.note: Sounds plausible, but the text says no pedals.

another.text: Wrong answers on detail questions are usually things that sound true or that you already believe. The test is checking whether you'll trust the passage over your memory. Always trust the passage.
another.example:
Text: pedals added in the 1860s
Ask: when were pedals added?
Answer: the 1860s, even if you thought it was earlier.

questions.passage: Sea otters sleep floating on their backs. To keep from drifting apart, they hold paws or wrap themselves in kelp. A group of resting otters is called a raft.
questions.stem: According to the text, why do otters hold paws?
questions.why: The text says it directly: "To keep from drifting apart, they hold paws."

questions.passage: The school garden produced 300 pounds of vegetables last year. Most of it went to the cafeteria. The rest was sold at a Saturday market, and the money bought seeds for this spring.
questions.stem: What did the market money pay for?
questions.why: "The money bought seeds for this spring." Finger on the words.

questions.passage: Marco trained for the race for six months. He ran before school three days a week and swam on the weekends. On race day it rained, and he finished fourth.
questions.stem: How often did Marco run?
questions.why: "He ran before school three days a week." The weekends were for swimming.

questions.passage: Venus is the hottest planet, even though Mercury is closer to the sun. A thick blanket of clouds traps heat on Venus, so its surface stays around 870 degrees Fahrenheit day and night.
questions.stem: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
options: It is closer to the sun.
questions.why: "A thick blanket of clouds traps heat." Mercury is closer, and the text says Venus is still hotter.

questions.passage: The bakery opens at six, but the line starts forming at five thirty. The first fifty customers get a free coffee. By seven, the cinnamon rolls are usually gone.
questions.stem: What do the first fifty customers get?
questions.why: "The first fifty customers get a free coffee." Cinnamon rolls are mentioned, but not as the prize.

name: Inference
sub: What the text means but doesn't say
rule: An inference is a conclusion the clues in the text force you to. It is not stated, but it is the only thing that makes sense given what is stated.
trick: Ask: which answer would the author nod along to? The right inference adds one small step. Wrong ones add a leap the text never set up.
passage: When Ana opened the door, the dog did not run to greet her. His bowl was still full from the morning, and he lifted his head only long enough to sigh.

examples.text: The dog is probably sick or sad.
examples.note: No greeting, no eating, sighing. The clues point there.

examples.text: The dog ran away later that night.
examples.note: Nothing in the text sets that up.

another.text: Think like a detective. You never saw the crime, but the muddy footprints and the open window let you say what happened. An inference uses the footprints in the text. A guess ignores them.
another.example:
Clues: full bowl, no greeting, a sigh
Inference: something is wrong with the dog
Guess: the dog is old

questions.passage: Priya checked the weather app three times before leaving. She packed an umbrella, a second pair of socks, and a plastic bag for her phone.
questions.stem: What can you infer?
questions.why: Umbrella, dry socks, a bag to keep the phone dry. Every clue points to rain.

questions.passage: The restaurant had no sign and no menu. Regulars just nodded at the cook, who already knew their order. A tourist who wandered in stood by the door for a full minute before anyone noticed him.
questions.stem: What can you infer about the restaurant?
options: It is about to close for good.
It mostly serves people who already know it.
The food is not very good.
questions.why: No sign, no menu, regulars who don't need to order. It runs on people who already know the place.

questions.passage: By the third mile, Jamal had stopped checking his watch. He was humming, and when a runner passed him, he smiled and waved instead of speeding up.
questions.stem: What can you infer about Jamal?
options: He is about to drop out of the race.
He is not worried about his time.
questions.why: He stopped checking his watch and let someone pass without caring. Time isn't his goal today.

questions.passage: The classroom plants on the window side had grown twice as tall as the ones near the door. Both groups got the same water and the same soil.
questions.stem: What most likely explains the difference?
options: The door plants got too much water.
The window plants got more light.
questions.why: Water and soil were the same, so the only difference left is the window. Windows mean light.

questions.passage: Grandpa kept every birthday card in a shoebox, sorted by year. The oldest were soft at the edges from being handled. He could tell you who sent each one without looking at the signature.
questions.stem: What can you infer about Grandpa?
options: The cards mean a great deal to him.
questions.why: Saving, sorting, handling them often, remembering each sender. All of it shows how much he values them.

name: Words in context
sub: What a word means in this sentence
rule: A word can mean different things in different sentences. The surrounding words tell you which meaning is being used here.
trick: Cover the word. Read the sentence and say your own word for the blank. Then pick the answer closest to your word.
passage: The committee tabled the proposal until spring, when more members could attend.

examples.text: Here, "tabled" means postponed.
examples.note: Cover it: the committee ___ the proposal until spring. Put off.

examples.text: "Tabled" means put on a table.
examples.note: The everyday meaning doesn't fit "until spring."

another.text: The test picks words with a common meaning and a less common one, then uses the less common one. If the obvious meaning makes the sentence silly, it's the other meaning.
another.example:
"The novel's plot was thin."
Not skinny. Weak, lacking detail.

questions.passage: After the flood, the town had to address the broken bridge before anything else.
questions.stem: In this sentence, "address" most nearly means:
questions.why: Cover it: the town had to ___ the broken bridge. Deal with. You can't speak to a bridge.

questions.passage: Her argument was sound, and even the people who disagreed with her admitted it.
questions.stem: In this sentence, "sound" most nearly means:
questions.why: An argument that opponents admit is good is solid or well-reasoned. Noise doesn't fit.

questions.passage: The coach was blunt: the team had not practiced enough, and it showed.
questions.stem: In this sentence, "blunt" most nearly means:
questions.why: What follows the colon is plain, honest talk. Direct. A knife is dull; a person is direct.

questions.passage: The museum's new wing will house the photography collection.
questions.stem: In this sentence, "house" most nearly means:
questions.why: A wing of a building that will ___ a collection. Hold or contain it.

questions.passage: Scientists have observed a marked drop in the bird's population since 2010.
questions.stem: In this sentence, "marked" most nearly means:
questions.why: A ___ drop that scientists observed. A clear, noticeable one. Nothing is being written on.

name: Why the author wrote it
rule: Purpose is what the author wants the sentence or passage to do: give information, convince you of something, tell a story, or explain how something works.
trick: Ask "what is this sentence doing for the paragraph?" Giving an example? Setting up a contrast? Answering a question raised earlier? Name the job, not the topic.
passage: Most people assume spiders are insects. They are not. Insects have six legs and three body parts; spiders have eight legs and two. The difference matters to scientists, who group them in separate classes.

examples.text: The third sentence explains the difference the second sentence claimed.
examples.note: Its job is to back up "They are not."

examples.text: The third sentence is about legs.
examples.note: That's the topic, not the purpose.

another.text: Every sentence in a good paragraph has a job: claim, evidence, example, contrast, or conclusion. Purpose questions ask for the job title. Look at the sentence before and after to see what it's doing for them.
another.example:
Claim: Spiders aren't insects.
Evidence: 8 legs vs 6, 2 parts vs 3.
Why it matters: separate classes.

questions.passage: Ice cream sales rise in the summer. So do drownings. That does not mean ice cream causes drowning; both go up because more people are at the beach when it is hot.
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To warn people about eating before swimming
To explain why two things can rise together without one causing the other
To describe summer at the beach
questions.why: The ice cream example exists to make a point about cause. The last sentence states that point.

questions.passage: You should learn to cook at least five meals before you move out. Takeout is expensive, and a person who can feed themselves is never stuck.
questions.stem: What is the author's purpose?
options: To persuade the reader to learn to cook
To describe the cost of takeout
questions.why: "You should" is the giveaway. The reasons that follow are there to convince you.

questions.passage: The lighthouse keeper's job was simple and relentless. Every evening at dusk, she climbed 112 steps to light the lamp. Every morning she climbed them again to put it out, then polished the glass until the sun was high.
questions.stem: What does the second sentence do in the passage?
options: It gives an example of what "relentless" means.
It argues that the job should be automated.
questions.why: The first sentence makes a claim (relentless). The climbing-112-steps detail shows it.

questions.passage: Some people think the moon has a dark side that never sees the sun. In fact, every part of the moon gets sunlight; we just only ever see one side from Earth.
questions.stem: What is the purpose of the first sentence?
options: To state a common belief the author will correct
To explain how the moon orbits
To describe what the author believes
questions.why: "Some people think" followed by "In fact" is the classic setup: present the myth, then fix it.

questions.passage: The recipe calls for cold butter. Cold butter makes small pockets in the dough that turn to steam in the oven, and that steam is what makes a pie crust flaky.
questions.stem: What does the second sentence do?
options: It explains why the first sentence's instruction matters.
It disagrees with the first sentence.
questions.why: First sentence: do this. Second sentence: here's why. Explanation.

name: How the text is built
sub: Problem and solution, compare, cause and effect, sequence
rule: Passages are built in a few shapes: a problem then its solution, two things compared, a cause and its effects, or events in order. Spotting the shape tells you how the parts connect.
trick: Look for the signal words. But, however, unlike = comparing. Because, so, as a result = cause and effect. First, then, finally = sequence. The problem is, one fix = problem and solution.
passage: City buses were always late because they sat in the same traffic as cars. So the city painted one lane red and reserved it for buses. Within a month, the average trip was eight minutes shorter.

examples.text: Problem (late buses), solution (bus lane), result (shorter trips).
examples.note: "Because" and "So" mark the joints.

examples.text: A comparison of buses and cars.
examples.note: Cars are mentioned, but nothing is being compared.

another.text: Picture the paragraph as a diagram. Problem and solution is an arrow from a bad thing to a fix. Compare is two columns. Cause and effect is dominoes. Sequence is a timeline. Which diagram would you draw?
another.example:
late buses → red lane → 8 min faster
That's an arrow: problem to solution to result.

questions.passage: A hurricane is a tropical storm with winds over 74 miles per hour. A typhoon is the same kind of storm. The only difference is where it happens: hurricanes form in the Atlantic, typhoons in the western Pacific.
questions.stem: How is this passage organized?
options: As a comparison of two things
As a problem and a solution
questions.why: Two storms, side by side, with the one difference pointed out. Comparison.

questions.passage: First, soak the beans overnight. The next morning, drain them and cover with fresh water. Simmer for an hour, then add salt only at the end, or the skins will toughen.
questions.stem: How is this passage organized?
questions.why: First, next morning, then, at the end. A sequence of steps.

questions.passage: Because the river flooded every spring, farmers along it lost their crops. So they built levees. The levees worked, but they also kept the river from spreading new soil on the fields, and over time the land grew less fertile.
questions.stem: What does the last sentence add to the passage?
options: A second problem caused by the solution
The first step in a process
questions.why: The levees fixed the flooding and created a new problem. The passage keeps following causes to their effects.

questions.passage: Unlike most birds, penguins cannot fly. Their wings have become flippers, and while this makes them clumsy on land, it makes them fast and agile underwater.
questions.stem: Which words signal the passage's structure?
questions.why: "Unlike" compares penguins to other birds; "while" compares land and water. Those are comparison signals.

questions.passage: Students kept forgetting their locker combinations in September. The school tried posting reminders, which did nothing. Then it let students pick their own combinations, and the problem mostly disappeared.
questions.stem: How is this passage organized?
options: A problem, a failed fix, then a fix that worked
questions.why: Problem, first attempt, second attempt. Problem and solution with a false start.

name: Comparing two texts
sub: Where two authors agree and disagree
rule: When two short texts are paired, the question usually asks how Author 2 would react to Author 1. Find each author's main claim first, then compare them.
trick: Write one line for each author: "Author 1 thinks ___. Author 2 thinks ___." The answer is the relationship between those two lines: agree, disagree, or agree with a condition.
passage:
Text 1: Homework helps students practice what they learned in class and builds responsibility.

Text 2: Studies show homework has little effect on learning before high school. Younger students benefit more from sleep and play.

examples.text: Author 2 would say homework is less useful for younger kids than Author 1 claims.
examples.note: Author 2 doesn't reject homework entirely, just for younger students.

examples.text: Author 2 thinks homework should be banned.
examples.note: Too strong. Text 2 says "before high school," not never.

another.text: Wrong answers go too far. If Text 2 offers a caution, the answer isn't "completely disagrees." If Text 2 adds a detail, the answer isn't "proves Text 1 wrong." Match the strength of the answer to the strength of the text.
another.example:
Text 2 says "little effect before high school"
→ partial disagreement, not total.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Electric cars produce no exhaust, so switching to them will cut city air pollution.

Text 2: Electric cars do cut exhaust, but the electricity still has to come from somewhere. In cities powered by coal plants, the pollution moves rather than disappears.
questions.stem: How would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Text 1?
options: By saying the benefit depends on how the electricity is made
By arguing that electric cars pollute more than gas cars
questions.why: Text 2 accepts the exhaust point and adds a condition about the power source. Not total agreement, not reversal.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Reading on a screen is just as good as reading on paper. Words are words.

Text 2: In several experiments, people remembered more of what they read on paper, especially for long texts.
questions.stem: What would the author of Text 2 say about Text 1's claim?
options: It is supported by the experiments.
It ignores evidence that paper works better for long reading.
It applies only to short texts.
questions.why: Text 2 brings evidence against "just as good," at least for long texts. It challenges the claim.

questions.passage:
Text 1: The best way to learn a language is to live where it is spoken.

Text 2: Living abroad helps, but only if the learner actually speaks with locals. Plenty of people spend a year in another country and come home with the same fifty words.
questions.stem: The two authors would most likely agree that:
options: Living abroad is useless for learning a language.
Being in the country can help a learner.
Fifty words is enough to get by.
questions.why: Text 1 says it's the best way; Text 2 says it helps if you talk to people. Both agree it can help.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Zoos protect endangered animals by breeding them safely.

Text 2: Breeding programs have saved a few species, but most zoo animals are not endangered, and the money might protect more animals if spent on wild habitats.
questions.stem: How does Text 2 relate to Text 1?
options: It gives more examples of what Text 1 says.
It accepts part of Text 1 and questions the rest.
It says the opposite of Text 1.
questions.why: Text 2 grants that some species were saved, then questions whether zoos are the best use of the money.

questions.passage:
Text 1: Daily quizzes make students study more consistently.

Text 2: Daily quizzes do raise study time. They also raise stress, and for some students the stress cancels out the gain.
questions.stem: On which point do the two authors agree?
options: Quizzes lead students to study more.
questions.why: Text 2's second sentence repeats Text 1's claim before adding the downside.

name: Tone
sub: How the author feels about it
rule: Tone is the author's attitude toward the subject. You hear it in word choice: the same fact can be described with admiring, mocking, worried, or neutral words.
trick: Pull out the two or three words with the most feeling. Are they warm, cold, scared, or flat? That's the tone. If the words are plain and factual, the tone is neutral.
passage: The old theater, with its peeling gold paint and seats that still smell faintly of popcorn from 1975, is the best place in town to watch a movie.

examples.text: Affectionate.
examples.note: "Faintly of popcorn from 1975" and "best place" are fond, not critical.

examples.text: Critical.
examples.note: Peeling paint sounds negative, but the sentence ends by praising the place.

another.text: Read the sentence out loud the way the author would say it. Would they smile, roll their eyes, lower their voice? Your face tells you the tone before you have the word for it.
another.example:
"Yet another sequel nobody asked for" → eye roll → sarcastic
"The engine produces 300 horsepower" → flat → neutral

questions.passage: Once again the city council has promised to fix the potholes "soon." Residents who have heard this every spring for a decade have started planting flowers in them.
questions.stem: What is the tone of the passage?
questions.why: "Once again," quotes around "soon," and flowers in the potholes. The author is mocking the council.

questions.passage: The glacier has lost a third of its mass since 1980. At the current rate, the lake it feeds will be dry within our children's lifetimes.
questions.stem: What is the tone of the passage?
questions.why: "A third of its mass," "dry," "our children's lifetimes." The author wants you worried.

questions.passage: The new bridge spans 1,200 feet and carries four lanes of traffic. It opened in March after three years of construction.
questions.stem: What is the tone of the passage?
questions.why: Numbers and dates, no feeling words. Plain reporting.

questions.passage: Watching her solve the puzzle was like watching water find its way downhill: no wasted motion, no hesitation, just an easy certainty about where to go next.
questions.stem: What is the author's attitude toward "her"?
questions.why: "No wasted motion," "easy certainty." The water comparison is a compliment.

questions.passage: I suppose the restaurant was fine, if you enjoy waiting forty minutes for a lukewarm sandwich and a waiter who sighs when you ask for water.
questions.stem: What is the tone?
questions.why: "I suppose," "if you enjoy," lukewarm, sighing. Every detail is a complaint dressed as a compliment.

name: Does it support the claim?
sub: Evidence that actually backs up the point
rule: Evidence supports a claim only if it points the same direction as the claim. A fact can be true and interesting and still not support anything.
trick: Say the claim, then "because," then the evidence. If the sentence sounds like a real reason, it supports. If it sounds like a change of subject, it doesn't.
passage: Claim: The new crosswalk made the intersection safer.

examples.text: Accidents at the intersection fell from 12 a year to 3.
examples.note: Safer, because accidents dropped. Real reason.

examples.text: The crosswalk cost $40,000.
examples.note: True, but it says nothing about safety.

another.text: Imagine arguing with a skeptic. The claim is yours. Which fact would make the skeptic say "okay, fair point"? That's the supporting evidence. A fact the skeptic could shrug at supports nothing.
another.example:
Skeptic: "Safer? Prove it."
You: "Accidents went from 12 to 3."
Skeptic: "Fair."

questions.passage: Claim: Students who eat breakfast do better in morning classes.
questions.stem: Which finding best supports the claim?
options: Students who ate breakfast scored 10% higher on 9 a.m. quizzes than those who skipped it.
Most students prefer cereal to eggs.
questions.why: Better in the morning, because breakfast-eaters scored higher on morning quizzes. The other two change the subject.

questions.passage: Claim: The town's recycling program is working.
questions.stem: Which finding best supports the claim?
options: Trash sent to the landfill has dropped 30% since the program began.
Some residents say the bins are too small.
questions.why: Working, because less trash goes to the landfill. The start date proves nothing; the complaint cuts the other way.

questions.passage: Claim: Bees are drawn to blue flowers more than red ones.
questions.stem: Which finding best supports the claim?
options: Blue flowers tend to bloom in spring.
In a garden with equal numbers of each, bees visited blue flowers three times as often.
questions.why: A fair comparison with a clear result. Eye count and bloom time don't address preference.

questions.passage: Claim: The library's late-night hours are popular with students.
questions.stem: Which finding would weaken the claim?
options: On a typical night after 10 p.m., fewer than five people are in the building.
The library added more outlets last year.
Students can also study in the student center.
questions.why: Popular means people show up. Almost nobody showing up points the opposite way.

questions.passage: Claim: Practicing an instrument a little every day works better than one long weekly session.
questions.stem: Which finding best supports the claim?
options: Students who practiced 20 minutes daily learned a piece faster than students who practiced 2 hours once a week.
Daily practice is harder to schedule.
questions.why: Same total time, split differently, with a result. That's a direct test of the claim.

name: Finishing the thought
sub: Which ending follows from what came before
rule: When a text ends in a blank, the right ending is the one the earlier sentences were building toward. It should feel like the natural next step, not a new idea.
trick: Read everything before the blank and predict the ending in your own words before looking at the choices. Then pick the choice that matches your prediction.
passage: Desert plants lose water through their leaves. Cactuses have no leaves at all, only spines, which have almost no surface area. This design most likely helps a cactus ______

examples.text: hold on to water.
examples.note: Leaves lose water, cactuses have none, so they keep water. The chain leads here.

examples.text: attract pollinators.
examples.note: A new idea. Nothing before the blank was about pollinators.

another.text: The sentences before the blank are a staircase. The right answer is the next stair. Wrong answers are a different staircase entirely, or they jump three steps ahead to something the text never set up.
another.example:
Stair 1: leaves lose water.
Stair 2: cactus has no leaves.
Next stair: cactus loses less water.

questions.passage: Lighthouses were once staffed by keepers who lived on site. Today nearly all of them run on automatic lights and timers. As a result, the keeper's cottages ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: are now mostly empty or turned into museums.
were never built in the first place.
questions.why: No keepers means nobody in the cottages. Empty or repurposed follows directly.

questions.passage: A hummingbird's heart beats over a thousand times a minute, and it burns energy faster than almost any other animal. To survive, a hummingbird must ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.why: Burning energy fast means needing fuel fast. Constant eating is the next step.

questions.passage: The old map labeled the island as uninhabited. But researchers found stone walls, fire pits, and fish bones piled in neat heaps. The evidence suggests that ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the island has no fresh water.
people lived on the island at some point.
questions.why: Walls, fire pits, and food remains are signs of people. That corrects the map's label.

questions.passage: Most of a car's fuel is spent fighting air resistance at highway speeds. Engineers have found that lowering a car's height by a few inches reduces that resistance. Therefore, lower cars tend to ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: use less fuel on the highway.
questions.why: Less air resistance means less fuel fighting it. The text set up exactly that chain.

questions.passage: The town's only grocery store closed in June. The nearest one is now a forty-minute drive. Since many older residents do not drive, the closing has made it ______
questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: easier for them to shop locally.
harder for them to get food.
more likely they will move to the city.
questions.why: Store gone, next one far, no car. Harder to get food is the next stair. Moving to the city jumps too far.

name: Cause and effect
rule: A cause is why something happened. An effect is what happened because of it. The text usually gives you both; the question asks you to match them up.
trick: Find the signal: because, since, so, as a result, led to, due to. The cause is on the "because" side. The effect is on the "so" side.
passage: Because the river froze early, the ferry stopped running, so the island's school closed for a week.

examples.text: Cause: river froze. Effect: ferry stopped. Then that caused the school to close.
examples.note: A chain of two.

examples.text: The school closing caused the ferry to stop.
examples.note: Backwards. Check which side of "so" each one is on.

another.text: Ask "why?" to walk backward to the cause and "and then what?" to walk forward to the effect. Why did the school close? The ferry stopped. And then what happened after the river froze? The ferry stopped.
another.example:
Why did the ferry stop? ← the river froze (cause)
Ferry stopped, and then? → school closed (effect)

questions.passage: The drought dried the reservoir to a quarter of its usual level. As a result, the city banned lawn watering, and golf courses let their fairways go brown.
questions.stem: What caused the city to ban lawn watering?
questions.why: Low reservoir, "as a result," the ban. Brown fairways are another effect, not the cause.

questions.passage: Lena stayed up until two finishing her project. The next morning she slept through her alarm and missed the bus, so her mother had to drive her.
questions.stem: Why did Lena miss the bus?
questions.why: "She slept through her alarm and missed the bus." The late night is the cause behind that cause.

questions.passage: When wolves were brought back to the park, the deer stopped grazing in open valleys where they were easy to catch. Willows along the streams, which the deer had eaten down for decades, began to grow back.
questions.stem: What effect did the wolves have on the willows?
questions.why: Wolves → deer avoid valleys → willows stop being eaten → willows grow back. A chain of effects.

questions.passage: The factory began paying for bus passes. Within a year, fewer workers were late, and the company said it had saved money on overtime.
questions.stem: According to the text, what led to fewer late workers?
questions.why: The passes came first; lateness dropped after. The overtime savings are a further effect.

questions.passage: Because the gym raised its prices, Devon canceled his membership. He started running in the park instead, and he says he actually works out more now.
questions.stem: What was one effect of the price increase?
options: Devon began running in the park.
questions.why: Price up → canceled → ran in the park. The text says he works out more, not less.

name: Order of events
sub: What happened first, next, and last
rule: Stories don't always tell events in the order they happened. Time words and verb tenses tell you the real order.
trick: Watch for "had," "before," "earlier," and "by the time." They mean the event happened before whatever the text was just describing.
passage: When Sam reached the station, the train had already left. He had spent ten minutes looking for his ticket at home.

examples.text: Order: searched for ticket, train left, Sam arrived.
examples.note: "Had already left" and "had spent" both point backward.

examples.text: Order: Sam arrived, then the train left.
examples.note: "Had already left" means the train was gone before he got there.

another.text: Draw a quick timeline with three dots and place each event on it as you read. Anything with "had" goes to the left of where you are. Anything with "later" or "afterward" goes to the right.
another.example:
ticket search ← train leaves ← Sam arrives
(reading order was the reverse)

questions.passage: By the time the firefighters arrived, the neighbors had already carried the dog out and were spraying the porch with a garden hose.
questions.stem: What happened first?
options: The neighbors carried the dog out.
questions.why: "Had already carried" happened before the firefighters came, and the spraying was ongoing when they arrived.

questions.passage: Maya opened the envelope with shaking hands. Three months earlier she had mailed the application without telling anyone, certain she would be rejected.
questions.stem: Which event happened first?
questions.why: "Three months earlier she had mailed" places the mailing well before the envelope. Rejection never happens in the text.

questions.passage: The bakery sold out by nine. Later that afternoon, a second batch came out of the oven, and the line formed again before the bread had cooled.
questions.stem: What happened last?
questions.why: Sold out, then "later" the second batch, then the line. The line is the final event.

questions.passage: After the storm passed, Theo went out to check the boat. He had tied it to the dock the night before with two extra lines, and it was still there.
questions.stem: Put these in order: (A) Theo checks the boat, (B) the storm passes, (C) Theo ties the boat.
questions.why: He tied it "the night before," the storm passed, then he checked. C, B, A.

questions.passage: The team celebrated at midfield. Only an hour earlier, they had been down by two goals, and the coach had already started planning next week's practice.
questions.stem: What happened first?
options: The team was down by two goals.
The coach planned next week's practice.
questions.why: "An hour earlier, they had been down" comes first; the coach's planning came while they were down; the celebration came last.
